title: Why Kitchen Sinks Block: Grease in the P-Trap
description: When liquid cooking fats and oils enter your kitchen drain, they flow easily while warm. However, once they reach the standing water seal inside the cool P-trap, they rapidly cool and solidify into a sticky coating along the pipe walls. Over time, this grease layer catches fine food scraps, gradually reducing the internal pipe diameter until drainage slows or stops entirely. Rinsing with hot water often only pushes liquified grease slightly deeper down the line. To protect your drainage pipes, always wipe greasy cookware with paper towels into the trash before washing. What method do you use to manage kitchen grease?

A clean sectional cutaway view of the P-trap's lower curve clearly shows a dense layer of solidified yellow-brown grease and tiny trapped organic debris lining the interior pipe wall, noticeably constricting the liquid flow channel. Realistic plastic pipe texture, accurate threaded trap nuts, and realistic water level inside the trap bend. Clean surrounding environment inside an under-sink cabinet with soft, professional studio lighting highlighting the internal cross-section. Ample clean visual space at the top and bottom for text placement. Photorealistic style, visually accurate plumbing geometry, no text, no logos, no watermarks, no fake labels, no arrows.
visual_story: The visual uses a clear, realistic cross-sectional cutaway of a kitchen P-trap beneath the sink. Viewers can immediately see the interior of the pipe bend where standing water normally resides, highlighting a thick build-up of solidified fat and debris restricting the pipe's internal diameter. This visual clearly demonstrates where the majority of kitchen sink clogs originate and how grease physically accumulates inside drain fittings.

on_image_text.explanation: Liquid fats cool down and solidify inside the cold water seal of the P-trap, narrowing the drain.
on_image_text.takeaway: Scrape fats into the trash—never pour liquid oil or pan drippings down the drain.
